newsitem.title: USA: Bidding is tepid at big FCC wireless auction.
newsitem.headline: Bidding is tepid at big FCC wireless auction.

text.p: After skyrocketing earlier this year, prices for a slice of airwaves that will carry a new generation of cellular phone service have veered back toward earth at the latest, and largest, government auction.
Bids at the Federal Communications Commission's latest sale of new wireless phone permits were running at nearly a tenth the value of the average bid at a high-flying sale ended in May.
"The prices are extraordinarily low by any standard," said Jonathan Foxman of BIA Consulting Inc. in Chantilly, Va.
The auction passed the $1 billion mark on Monday, after 27 rounds of bidding by companies wanting to offer personal communications service, or PCS as the new service is called.
But bidding lags the $10.2 billion the government raised at its "C-Block" auction that ended in May, which was reserved for smaller companies.
That sale passed $3 billion after 13 rounds. Analysts said prices then were unrealistically high. The FCC raised $7.7 billion at its first PCS auction in 1995.

PCS technology is expected to turn the wireless phone into a mass-market product, allowing consumers to use different communications services -- such as phone, paging, fax and Internet access -- through a single hand-held device.
Units of Sprint Corp. and AT&T Corp. lead the latest bidding.
Analysts cited an oversupply of companies wanting to break into the PCS market and the smaller airwave parcels the FCC is auctioning as among the factors behind the slower bidding.
They also cited the slow speed some major winners from the C-Block auction -- including NextWave Telecom Inc. and General Wireless Inc. -- face in raising money to proceed with plans.
"The sources of finance are limited," said Mark Lowenstein of Yankee Group Inc., a Boston consulting firm.

As of Wednesday midday, the FCC had raised $1.09 billion after nearly a month of bidding. The sale involves 145 bidders vying for 1,479 PCS licenses in markets across the nation. It is the largest number of licenses offered simultaneously.
Current bids are "much more rational in terms of what people can make in these markets," said economist David Roddy of Deloitte & Touche Consulting Group.

Based on 1995 population sizes covered by the licenses, companies at the C-Block sale on average paid $37.97 a person. Today, bidders currently are offering the equivalent of about $4 a person for a similar airwave parcel, said BIA's Foxman.
While the latest auction is not expected to meet the rich prices paid earlier, Foxman still held out the prospect that bidding could pick up.
"It's early in the process and prices may well go up substantially. But I don't expect it will reach the prices in the C-Block," he said.
Analysts said the cheaper prices reflect several factors:
-- The airwave chunks being sold in the current auction, at 10 MHz a piece, are a third smaller and so less attractive than the 30 MHz slices sold in the two previous PCS auctions.
-- The PCS market is becoming overcrowded with new players and a price war looms. That leaves little room for relative newcomers to turn a profit.
-- Some winners in the C-Block auction are not having an easy time raising the money to fund their ventures, after plunking down bids ranging into the billions of dollars.

San Diego-based Nextwave -- which placed winning bids of $4.2 billion -- filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June to offer $300 million worth of stock and $400 million in bonds. The offerings have yet to proceed.

"The high-yield debt market has been extremely chilly to the C-Block players," said Steve Zecola, a top executive at US 1 Communications Corp., who earlier led a company that dropped out of the C-Block auction after prices in his opinion became too expensive.
A NextWave spokeswoman declined to comment, citing SEC rules about discussing a securities filing.
Corey Linquist of Dallas-based General Wireless, which has filed with the SEC to offer $165 million in stock and $220 million in bonds, said, "We're happy where we're at."
